title: Dynamic memory management
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe whether candidates can allocate, resize, and free heap memory without leaks, dangling pointers, or undefined behavior.

phases.goal: Establish why the heap exists and what malloc, calloc, and free provide.

must_hit.point: The stack is fast but constrains size (mostly compile-time), rigid lifetimes (cannot return a pointer to a local), and space (typically small; a huge stack array can overflow).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts stack/static duration with heap allocation requested at runtime.

must_hit.point: malloc(size) allocates size bytes of uninitialized memory and returns a pointer to it, or NULL on failure (OOM).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions uninitialized bytes and NULL check before use.

must_hit.point: calloc(nmemb, size) allocates for an array of nmemb elements of size bytes each and initializes all bytes to zero.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts calloc zero-init with malloc's uninitialized block.

must_hit.point: free(ptr) deallocates memory from malloc/calloc/realloc; if ptr is null, no action occurs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States free is a no-op on NULL and only frees allocator-returned blocks.

must_hit.point: Do not cast malloc in C: void* promotes to any pointer type; a cast can mask a missing #include <stdlib.h> (especially in C89).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says casting is unnecessary in C and risky for hiding undeclared malloc.

probes: Why use the heap instead of a stack array or VLA?
What does malloc return on failure, and how does calloc differ?

hints.1: Think about what happens when size is unknown until runtime or data must outlive the function.
hints.2: Name the four stdlib.h functions and contrast malloc vs calloc initialization.
hints.3: Heap from OS at runtime; malloc uninitialized or NULL; calloc zero-fills; free releases; no cast of malloc in C.

phases.goal: Explain the allocation/free contract, dangling pointers, and safe realloc behavior.

must_hit.point: Every successful allocation must be paired with exactly one free.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States one free per successful alloc as the memory contract.

must_hit.point: free does not erase the block's data and does not set the caller's pointer to NULL; after free(p), p is a dangling pointer and using it is undefined behavior—set p = NULL after free.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes dangling pointer and NULL-defuse after free.

must_hit.point: realloc may grow in place or allocate a new block, copy data, and free the old block; on failure it returns NULL and leaves the original block untouched.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains in-place vs move, and that failure preserves the old pointer's block.

must_hit.point: Never write p = realloc(p, ...); use a temporary pointer and only assign on success, or a failed realloc overwrites p with NULL and leaks the original block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the temp-pointer pattern and names the leak on failure.

must_hit.point: If ptr is NULL, realloc(ptr, size) behaves like malloc(size); after a successful realloc that moves, other pointers into the old block become dangling.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions NULL-as-malloc and stale interior pointers after a move.

probes: What is wrong with p = realloc(p, new_size)?
After free(p), what is the state of p and the freed bytes?

hints.1: Ask what ownership you surrender at free, and what realloc does if it cannot grow.
hints.2: Separate success path (new pointer, possibly moved) from failure path (NULL, old block still valid).
hints.3: Use int *temp = realloc(arr, ...); if (!temp) keep/free arr; else arr = temp; always NULL after free.

phases.goal: Compare allocation strategies and why heap freedom has costs.

must_hit.point: VLAs stay stack-bound: they can crash if too large and vanish when the function returns, so they do not replace heap allocation for large or long-lived data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects VLAs for size/lifetime reasons vs malloc.

must_hit.point: 2-D as array-of-pointers (row pointers then each row) allows ragged rows and matrix[r][c] but needs loops to alloc/free and scatters rows (poor cache locality).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names N+1-style allocs, ragged arrays, and cache downside.

must_hit.point: 2-D as one contiguous flat block needs one malloc/one free and good cache behavior, but requires index math like row * cols + col.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts single allocation and manual indexing with pointer-of-pointers.

must_hit.point: realloc can often expand in place without copying, which is faster than always malloc + memcpy + free of a new block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers realloc for growth when in-place expansion is possible.

probes: How would you dynamically allocate a matrix, and what are the trade-offs?
Why prefer realloc over always allocating a new buffer yourself?

hints.1: Consider syntax convenience versus number of allocations and memory layout.
hints.2: Compare array-of-pointers vs one flat buffer; mention in-place realloc.
hints.3: Ragged + matrix[r][c] vs contiguous + row*cols+col; realloc may avoid a full copy.

phases.goal: Apply ownership, common UB bugs, tooling, and when heap allocation is banned.

must_hit.point: Classic bugs: memory leak (lose all pointers before free); double free (corrupts allocator metadata, often crashes); use-after-free (dangling write can corrupt unrelated data); freeing a non-heap or mid-block pointer (e.g. free(p+1)) destroys the heap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists leak, double-free, use-after-free, and invalid free targets.

must_hit.point: Ownership must be explicit: a function that returns malloced memory transfers free responsibility to the caller (document that the caller frees).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States caller-frees for returned heap pointers.

must_hit.point: Detect heap bugs with valgrind (Linux) or AddressSanitizer (e.g. gcc -fsanitize=address -g).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names valgrind and/or ASan for leaks, double-frees, OOB.

must_hit.point: Real-time/embedded often bans dynamic allocation: malloc time is non-deterministic, fragmentation can cause late OOM, and systems may lack virtual memory/OS OOM handling—prefer static buffers or fixed-size pools.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties ban to latency, fragmentation, and catastrophic OOM without VM.

must_hit.point: Heap fragmentation: total free space may be large while no contiguous block satisfies a request (allocator tracks free/used blocks; long-running alloc/free of mixed sizes).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains Swiss-cheese free space failing a large contiguous request.

probes: Walk through the big heap UB bugs and how you would catch them.
Why is malloc often banned in real-time embedded or aerospace software?

hints.1: Think about what breaks the every-alloc-one-free contract at runtime.
hints.2: Cover leak, double-free, use-after-free, invalid free; then latency/fragmentation for embedded.
hints.3: Pair alloc/free with clear ownership; use valgrind/ASan; embedded prefers static pools because malloc is non-deterministic and can fragment.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Heap for runtime-sized or outliving-the-function data; stack/VLA is fast but size/lifetime limited and VLAs vanish on return and can overflow if large.
Pointer rows: ragged arrays and matrix[r][c], but multiple alloc/free and poor locality. Flat block: one malloc/free and cache-friendly, but manual row*cols+col indexing.
Manual copy always moves; realloc may expand in place without copying, which is much faster when adjacent space is free.

tradeoffs.topic: Dynamic allocation vs static buffers / fixed pools (embedded)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Heap is flexible but non-deterministic and fragmentable; real-time/aerospace often mandates static globals or fixed-size pools for predictability and safety.

gotchas.trap: Using the pointer after free without nulling it (dangling pointer).
gotchas.correction: free does not clear data or the pointer; set p = NULL immediately after free and never dereference a freed address.

gotchas.trap: Writing p = realloc(p, new_size) on failure.
gotchas.correction: Failed realloc returns NULL but leaves the old block valid; assigning NULL to p leaks it—use a temporary, then assign only on success.
Unnecessary in C; in C89 a cast can hide a missing stdlib.h so malloc is assumed to return int and a 64-bit pointer can be truncated to 32-bit.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the old pointer stays valid after successful realloc, or keeping interior pointers into the old block.
gotchas.correction: Always use the pointer realloc returns; if the block moved, any pointers into the old block are dangling.

gotchas.trap: Passing a stack address or mid-block pointer to free.
gotchas.correction: Only free pointers exactly returned by malloc/calloc/realloc—not locals and not p+1 into a block.

gotchas.trap: Partial allocation failure without cleanup (e.g. struct allocated but inner buffer fails; or buffer allocated then fopen fails).
gotchas.correction: On error paths free everything already allocated before returning (free inner then outer; free buffer if file open fails).
